column3: Exact parallel: Yahya receives peace at birth, death, and resurrection in the same three-part wording.
Scriptural distortion and false speech about God do not clarify Jesus' declaration of peace.
Its denial of death, life, and resurrection provides a thematic contrast to Jesus' affirmed resurrection.
Continues Jesus' first-person speech and his living, blessed mission immediately before the focus ayah.
Immediately identifies the speaker as Jesus son of Mary and continues the surrounding narrative.
Explicitly affirms the resurrection that Jesus names as the third protected threshold.
Contrasts dead, nonliving beings with the coming resurrection, supporting the life-death-resurrection frame.
Mary's arrival carrying Jesus supplies the immediate birth setting for his speech.
Its denial that God begets or is begotten helps bound the sonship claims surrounding Jesus' birth.
The trumpet day gestures toward eschatology but does not specifically illuminate Jesus' resurrection declaration.
False statements about God are too general to serve as a useful neighbour here.
Shares the word peace, but its nocturnal setting is unrelated to Jesus' life-cycle declaration.
Being alive is only a broad lexical and thematic overlap with the focus ayah.
The claim of future wealth and children belongs to the later dispute and does not clarify Jesus' statement.
Rising up to commit violence uses a different sense of the root from resurrection.
General maternal pregnancy and birth offer only distant background for Jesus' extraordinary birth.
The accusation against Mary forms the immediate social context for Jesus' infant speech.
Its objection to resurrection after death contrasts directly with the focus ayah's assured rising alive.
A greeting of peace for followers of guidance shares a formula but not the life-death-resurrection claim.
Rejects the assertion that God has taken a child, a central doctrinal context of this Jesus passage.
Affirms God's power to create and resurrect all people, directly supporting the final clause of 19:33.
The Day's witnesses and mercy concern judgment generally, not Jesus' birth, death, or resurrection.
The later threat to record speech is in the same passage but adds little to the focus ayah itself.
Its repeated challenge to resurrection after death is a clear contrast to Jesus' certainty of being raised.
God sending a human messenger is unrelated to Jesus' statement about his own life stages.
The challenge to speak to an infant directly precipitates Jesus' first-person declaration.
Sending someone is not the resurrection sense needed for the focus ayah.
Explicitly asks whether one can emerge alive after death, closely paralleling the focus ayah's final threshold.
Moses' admission of error does not illuminate Jesus' birth, death, resurrection, or peace.
The sending and teaching of a messenger is a different use of the relevant root.
References to travel days and dwellings have no meaningful connection to the focus ayah.
The claim that the Merciful has taken a child continues the doctrinal issue surrounding Jesus' identity.
Resurrection and accounting expand the eschatological event Jesus names, though the focus is judgment.
The statement that the slain are living offers a distant life-after-death comparison.
Jesus' declaration that he is God's servant, given scripture and prophethood, begins the speech culminating in 19:33.
Its warning that people will be raised supports the resurrection clause, without the birth or peace themes.
The Sabbath narrative only shares generic references to days.
The crowding around God's servant does not clarify the focus ayah.
A prophetic greeting of peace is a remote formal parallel to peace being upon Jesus.
Parent and child language offers only a broad birth-related resonance.
Continues the passage's rebuttal of the claim that the Merciful has a child.
Calling to God and being Muslim does not clarify the specific declaration of peace over Jesus' life stages.
The request for a king and the command to fight are unrelated to the focus ayah.
Israel's scripture, judgment, and prophethood do not provide a close neighbour for this declaration.
The barrier until the day of resurrection gives a clear death-to-resurrection framework.
Maternal nursing and parental duties provide only distant background for birth.
Continues the immediate rejection of attributing a child to the Merciful.
The greeting of peace upon Moses and Aaron is a prophetic formula parallel to peace upon Jesus.
A concrete death and revival demonstrates the divine power presupposed by Jesus' rising alive.
Jesus' goodness to his mother immediately precedes and completes the same first-person speech.
Revival after death directly parallels the focus ayah's affirmation of resurrection.
Gathering blind on the Day of Resurrection gives only broad eschatological context.
The coming news for deniers does not illuminate Jesus' declaration.
Peace upon Elias is another prophetic salutation but has no life-cycle parallel.
Peace upon all messengers broadens the prophetic blessing formula used for Jesus.
Immediately continues Jesus' identity and rejects divine sonship in the same narrative sequence.
Delay until the resurrection day gives limited temporal background only.
The burden on the Day of Resurrection is general judgment context rather than a close parallel.
God's inheritance of earth and return of all to Him extends the passage's death-and-return horizon.
Compelled surrender at death concerns wrongdoing, not the peace or resurrection stated by Jesus.
The prayer not to be disgraced on the day of resurrection directly shares the eschatological threshold.
The dispute over joining a campaign has no meaningful connection to the focus ayah.
Its repeated deaths and lives make death and restoration of life an explicit shared theme.
The day of accounting is only broad background for the resurrection clause.
The statement that God is Jesus' and his hearers' Lord immediately follows his declaration.
The challenge about being raised after death closely contrasts with Jesus' confident statement.
A postponed day without further context does not clarify the focus ayah.
Addressing disbelievers has no relevant connection.
The command to die in submission has a distant death-related overlap only.
The curse until the Day of Judgment is general eschatological background.
The parties' dispute and warning of a great Day continue the immediate aftermath of Jesus' speech.
God explicitly gives life and causes death, supplying the divine framework for the focus ayah's sequence.
Peace as the greeting when believers meet God combines the focus ayah's peace and eschatological motifs.
The judgment scene of every community called to its record expands the final-day context.
Death in disbelief is only a remote contrast to the focus ayah's protected life stages.
The true dominion on that day supplies limited judgment-day context.
The coming of all to God on a specified day immediately extends the passage's eschatological warning.
A military peace settlement is unrelated to peace upon Jesus across life stages.
Cosmic upheaval on a day gives only broad final-day context.
Moses' fear of being denied is unrelated to the focus ayah.
Wishing for death to test an afterlife claim is a remote death-related comparison.
The wrongdoer's regret on a day of judgment is only broad eschatological context.
Moses being raised as a child supplies a distant childhood and birth resonance.
God causing death and then giving life closely states the sequence affirmed in the focus ayah.
God causes death and gives life, directly grounding the paired life-and-death language.
God causes a group to die and then revives them, a concrete resurrection parallel.
Directly concerns Jesus, his mother, his speech from the cradle, and his raising of the dead by God's permission.
Explicitly affirms that God will raise those in graves, directly supporting Jesus' resurrection statement.
The Master of the Day of Judgment gives a concise eschatological frame for being raised alive.
Death is unavoidable and is followed by return to God, closely supporting the focus ayah's death-and-return horizon.
The Day of Decision is only an abbreviated judgment-day reference.
The prohibited call for peace in a conflict is not related to peace upon Jesus.
Fear of punishment on a great day offers only general final-day context.
A greeting of peace by visitors is a different social use of the word.
Hud's refusal of payment does not illuminate the focus ayah.
Kindness to parents is a distant parallel to Jesus' goodness to his mother, not to 19:33 itself.
Fear resembling death in battle is unrelated to Jesus' life stages.
Sending a messenger before punishment is a different use of the root and theme.
The comparison of disbelievers has no relevant connection.
Those raised from their resting place recognize the fulfilled promise, directly paralleling being raised alive.
Begins the immediately preceding account of Mary, which supplies the narrative setting for Jesus' birth.
The angel's appearance to Mary initiates the annunciation that leads to the speaker's birth.
Mary's appeal for protection frames the extraordinary conception that precedes Jesus' declaration.
The angel announces the gift of a pure son, directly anticipating Jesus' birth.
Mary's question about an untouched conception establishes the exceptional birth behind 19:33.
The child is declared a sign and a decreed matter, directly defining the birth's significance.
Mary's conception advances the immediate narrative of Jesus' arrival.
Mary's labor at the palm tree gives the direct birth setting omitted from the candidate list.
The consoling call during childbirth continues the scene that leads to Jesus speaking.
Provision during labor completes the immediate birth sequence.
Mary's vow of silence creates the narrative condition for the infant Jesus to speak for himself.
Yahya's announced birth begins the earlier parallel whose threefold peace formula is repeated in 19:33.
Zakariyya's astonishment at a late birth forms a deliberate counterpart to Mary's extraordinary conception.
God's creation despite prior barrenness supports the divine power behind the two miraculous births.
Zakariyya's speech restriction parallels the speech-centered structure of the surrounding birth narratives.
Zakariyya's gesture after silence provides a nearby contrast to Jesus' infant speech.
The angels announce Jesus the Messiah, son of Mary, directly identifying the subject of 19:33.
Jesus speaking in the cradle is a direct parallel to his infant first-person speech in Surah Maryam.
God creates as He wills by saying Be, directly supporting the miraculous conception.
Jesus revives the dead by God's permission, strongly connecting his identity to life and resurrection.
God's statement about Jesus' death and raising directly bears on the death-and-raising sequence of 19:33.
The Adam comparison reinforces creation without ordinary paternal descent in the Jesus narrative.
The denial that Jesus was killed or crucified is a direct textual neighbour to his statement about death.
God raising Jesus to Himself directly relates to the focus ayah's resurrection horizon.
Its reference to Jesus' death provides a closely related, though interpretively contested, temporal connection.
Names Jesus as Messiah and God's word while rejecting exaggerated claims about him, matching the passage's doctrinal boundary.
Rejects worship of the Messiah son of Mary, directly clarifying the servant identity Jesus asserts nearby.
Calls Jesus and his mother mortal recipients of food, directly relevant to his human birth and death.
Jesus disavows telling people to worship him and his mother, extending the anti-deification context.
Jesus' testimony after God takes him directly concerns his earthly life and departure.
Mary's chastity, the breathing of spirit, and the mother-son sign directly support the miraculous birth context.
Calls Mary and her son a sign, offering a close Quranic parallel to the Maryam narrative.
Describes Jesus as a servant favored and made an example, reinforcing his non-divine identity.
Mary's chastity and reception of God's words provide another direct conception parallel.
Explicitly orders the sequence dead, given life, caused to die, revived, and returned to God.
God demonstrates revival of the dead to Abraham, directly supporting resurrection after death.
States that God will resurrect the dead and gather them back to Him.
Explicitly states that people live, die, and are brought forth again.
Answers the denial of resurrection with God's firm promise to raise the dead.
Presents the objection to being raised after death as bones and fragments.
Answers that objection by affirming the one who first created them will restore them.
States the human cycle of creation from earth, return to it, and being brought forth again.
Uses human creation and reviving dead earth as explicit evidence for resurrection.
Declares that God gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
States that God gives life, causes death, and will give life again.
States that human beings die after their worldly life.
Follows the death statement with explicit resurrection on the Day of Resurrection.
Links the first creation to repeating creation, supporting the possibility of resurrection.
States that God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him.
Names bringing the living from the dead and reviving the earth as a model for being brought forth.
Describes repeating creation as within God's power, supporting the resurrection clause.
Explicitly states that God gives life to the dead and records what they send ahead.
States the classic objection about who will revive decayed bones.
Answers that the original Creator will revive decayed bones.
The trumpet blast, death, and subsequent rising provide a direct collective resurrection scene.
States that God gives life and causes death, then brings His decree about.
States that God gives life and causes death before gathering all on the Day of Resurrection.
Records the objection that return after death and becoming dust is improbable.
States that God gives life and causes death, and that all return to Him.
Declares that the second creation belongs to God, directly supporting resurrection.
Appeals to the first creation as evidence for replacement and renewed creation.
States that God created death and life, grounding the focus ayah's two stated thresholds.
Directly rejects the assumption that God will not reassemble human bones.
Concludes that the Creator can give life to the dead.
Describes the single blast that initiates the final rising.
States that people then emerge awake on the surface of the earth.
Explicitly says that God will resurrect the human being when He wills.
The scattering of graves is a direct eschatological image of the dead being raised.
Names God as the one who originates and repeats creation.
Affirms God's power to return the human being after creation.
The birth and dedication of Mary supplies ancestral and maternal background to Jesus' birth narrative.
Mary's election and purification directly precede the annunciation of Jesus in this passage.
The unseen report of Mary establishes the narrative lead-in to Jesus' announced birth.
Names Jesus among the guided prophets, supporting the prophetic identity he declares in Surah Maryam.
Yahya's divinely granted wisdom extends the earlier birth narrative that 19:33 deliberately echoes.
Yahya's tenderness and purity continue the closely parallel account before the shared peace formula.
Yahya's goodness to his parents parallels the ethical character Jesus declares in the same speech.
The charge of attributing a child to the Merciful continues the doctrinal rebuttal immediately after Jesus' account.
The cosmic reaction intensifies the rejection of divine sonship in the same passage.
States that every being comes to the Merciful only as a servant, clarifying Jesus' servant identity.
God's complete enumeration of all beings reinforces their creaturely status in the anti-sonship passage.
Each creature's individual return to God extends the personal death-and-return horizon of 19:33.
The folding of heaven and repetition of creation provides a broad but explicit renewed-creation parallel.
God reviving dead earth is explicitly offered as the pattern for resurrection.
The trumpet blast and emergence from graves depict the collective raising that 19:33 anticipates.
God takes souls at death and later returns some, providing a close Quranic account of death under divine control.
God revives dead earth as evidence that He will give life to the dead.
The revival of dead land is explicitly compared to human emergence after death.
The denial that there is any death beyond the first and any resurrection directly contrasts with 19:33.
The Creator of heaven and earth is explicitly declared able to give life to the dead.
God brings forth a dead land and identifies it as the model for emergence from graves.
The argument from first creation rebuts doubt about renewed creation.
People emerge from graves with humbled eyes, a direct image of resurrection.
God gives life and causes death, directly supporting the focus ayah's life-and-death sequence.
People rush forth from graves, directly depicting the raising alive named in 19:33.
The trumpet is blown and people come forth in crowds, supplying a direct resurrection scene.
The earth casting out what is within it is a close image of graves yielding the dead.
The earth obeying its Lord completes the image of universal submission at resurrection.
